c1176: What you will find in this guide
c1177: ▸ The 25 points the inspector checks, with what they look at in each one and its category under the FDA Food Code (Priority / Priority foundation / Core).
c1178: ▸ An automatic summary that separates Priority violations from Priority foundation violations, counts the points left unanswered and calculates your compliance percentage.
c1179: ▸ What to do in the 24 hours before an inspection.
c1180: ▸ Which documents to have ready, in one binder and within reach.
c1181: ▸ The mistakes that get cited most, so none of them catches you out.
c1182: ▸ Based on the experience of John Guerrero: food service consultant since 2010, working in kitchens since he was 17.
c1184: ▸ Walk through the premises with the printed sheet or on your phone and mark each point with the drop-down: ✓ Compliant, ⚠ Needs work or ✗ Not compliant. They color themselves.
c1185: ▸ Look first at the "Priority violations" box: if it is not zero, that is what needs fixing today.
c1186: ▸ Repeat the self-assessment every quarter and keep the sheets. The series shows that you verify your own system, which is exactly what HACCP principle 6 asks for.
c1188: The FDA Food Code (2022), as adopted by your state or local health department, sorts violations into three categories. Priority: the item directly controls a hazard (cooking, cooling, hot and cold holding, handwashing). Priority foundation: it supports a Priority item (written plans, records, training, equipment). Core: general sanitation and facilities. Closure is not the normal consequence of a violation: it is reserved for an imminent health hazard (§8-404.11). The category is always decided by the inspector. UK: your local authority scores each inspection under the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme, from 0 to 5.
c1189: The 25 Points the Health Inspector Checks
c1190: Self-assess your establishment BEFORE the inspection. Below the table you have the automatic summary and three blocks: what to do in the last 24 hours, which documents to have ready and the mistakes that get cited most.
c1197: Hazard analysis, CCPs, critical limits, monitoring, corrective actions and verification (template 12 (HACCP Plan Template: Hazard Analysis & CCPs)). Food Code §8-201.13 says when a written plan is required; UK: Reg. 852/2004, art. 5.
c1199: Monitoring records up to date and signed
c1200: Temperature, cleaning, traceability and corrective action records for the past year, signed. FSMA 204: traceability records for foods on the Food Traceability List must reach the FDA within 24 hours (required from July 20, 2028). UK: "one step back, one step forward".
c1201: Food safety training documented by the business
c1202: Proof of training for every food handler and the training log (BONUS-01 (Food Safety Training Log)). The person in charge must be a Certified Food Protection Manager (CFPM, Food Code §2-102.12), plus a food handler card where your state requires it. UK: no legal certificate; Level 2 is the usual standard.
c1203: Allergen guide available and up to date
c1204: Available to any customer who asks, consistent with the allergen matrix (template 08 (Menu Allergen Matrix (US Big 9 & UK 14))) and the current menu. US: the 9 major allergens, in writing (Food Code §3-602.12); UK: the 14 allergens.
c1206: Contract with a licensed pest control operator, with license number and certificates
c1207: Contract in force, operator holding a state applicator license (UK: BPCA or NPTA member), a service report for every visit and the bait station map (template 07 (Pest Control Log & Bait Station Map))
c1210: On-site reading with the inspector's thermometer, checked against your template 01 (Food Temperature Log: Coolers, Freezers & Hot Holding)
c1212: On-site reading and food properly frozen, with no heavy frost and no signs of thawing and refreezing
c1214: Holding temperature of the hot dishes at the time of the visit (UK: 145 °F (63 °C) or above)
c1215: Clean, accessible probe thermometer in use
c1216: It exists, it is within reach, it is clean and staff know how to use it
c1219: Regular probe check in an ice bath or boiling water, with the deviation recorded (template 19 (Thermometer Calibration Log))
c1222: Floors, walls, ceilings and equipment free of grease buildup, including the back of the machinery
c1224: No cracks or damage, food-grade (smooth, durable, nonabsorbent) and easy to clean
c1225: Handwashing sink in the food prep area
c1226: Accessible and used only for handwashing, with hot water, soap, single-use paper towels and a foot-pedal trash can
c1227: Separation of dirty and clean areas
c1228: Workflow with no crossover between raw and cooked food, in space or in time
c1230: Street clothes kept apart from work clothes, lockers and cleanliness
c1232: Oldest stock in front; nothing past its date in the cooler or the storeroom, not even if it is "set aside to throw out"
c1233: Raw and cooked food kept apart
c1234: Never on the same shelf; raw food always below ready-to-eat food
c1236: Everything identified with its name, preparation date and use-by date
c1238: Everything on shelves or pallets, nothing directly on the floor
c1239: Cleaning products stored separately in a closed cabinet
c1240: Never next to food, in the original container with its label and its Safety Data Sheet (SDS)
c1243: Clean uniform, hair restraint, no jewelry (a plain ring band is allowed), closed-toe shoes, short nails and covered wounds
c1245: Total polar materials (TPM) test, oil change log (template 09 (Fryer Oil Log (TPM Tests & Disposal))) and a pickup receipt from a used-oil collector or recycler
c1247: In the refrigerator at 41 °F or below, covered and on a tray; never at room temperature, in standing water or under warm running water
c1249: Fish served raw, marinated or partly cooked: frozen at -4 °F for 168 hours or at -31 °F for 15 hours, with a log (template 18 (Parasite Destruction Log (Fish Served Raw))). UK/EU: 24 hours at -4 °F (-20 °C)
c1251: Trained staff, a written protocol and dedicated utensils when an allergy is declared (chart in template 14 (Allergen Chart & Allergic Reaction Protocol))
c1260: BEFORE THE INSPECTION: THE LAST 24 HOURS
c1261: Fill in this self-assessment yourself and fix whatever shows up red: the inspector is going to look at exactly the same things.
c1262: Bring this month's records up to date and sign them. A sheet without a signature counts as not done.
c1263: Check the temperatures of coolers, freezers and the steam table with a probe and enter them in template 01 (Food Temperature Log: Coolers, Freezers & Hot Holding).
c1264: Check use-by dates and the labeling of everything made in house.
c1265: Organize the walk-in: raw food at the bottom, everything covered, labeled and kept apart from ready-to-eat food.
c1266: Go over floor drains, the hood, door gaskets and the back of the equipment: that is where inspectors look once the obvious is clean.
c1267: Put cleaning products back in their closed cabinet and keep the Safety Data Sheets (SDS) within reach.
c1268: Decide who walks with the inspector and who keeps working. Choose someone who knows where every record is and does not improvise answers.

c1270: HACCP plan: hazard analysis (template 12 (HACCP Plan Template: Hazard Analysis & CCPs)) and cleaning & sanitizing schedule (template 03 (Master Cleaning & Sanitizing Schedule)) with its list of chemicals.
c1271: Temperature logs: daily (template 01 (Food Temperature Log: Coolers, Freezers & Hot Holding)) and receiving (template 02 (Receiving Temperature Log)) for the past year.
c1272: Receiving checklist (template 05 (Receiving Checklist for Deliveries)) together with its invoices / packing slips.
c1273: Traceability log for lots in and out (template 06 (Food Traceability Log (Lots In & Out))).
c1274: Daily cleaning checklist and weekly tasks (template 04 (Daily Cleaning Checklist (AM/PM))).
c1275: Pest control: contract with the operator's license number, a service report for every visit and the bait station map (template 07 (Pest Control Log & Bait Station Map)).
c1276: Fryer oil log (template 09 (Fryer Oil Log (TPM Tests & Disposal))) and used-oil pickup receipts.
c1277: Water quality log (template 10 (Water Quality Log (Chlorine & Private Supply))) and lab test reports if you have your own well or private water supply.
c1278: Allergen matrix (template 08 (Menu Allergen Matrix (US Big 9 & UK 14))) and the allergen guide available to customers.
c1279: Cooking and reheating logs (template 16 (Cooking & Reheating Temperature Log)), cooling and thawing logs (template 17 (Cooling & Thawing Log (2-Stage Cooling))) and parasite destruction logs (template 18 (Parasite Destruction Log (Fish Served Raw))); keep the parasite destruction records for 90 days (§3-402.12).
c1280: Thermometer calibration log (template 19 (Thermometer Calibration Log)), corrective action log (template 11 (Corrective Action Log)) and staff training log (BONUS-01 (Food Safety Training Log)).
c1281: THE MISTAKES THAT GET CITED MOST
c1282: Records filled in after the fact, all in the same handwriting and the same pen. It shows, and it wipes out the value of the whole series.
c1283: HACCP plan bought and left in a drawer, without a single signature and without a single corrective action recorded all year.
c1284: Food uncovered, unlabeled or with raw food above cooked food in the cooler.
c1285: Expired product in the cooler or the storeroom, even if it is "set aside to throw out": if it is inside, it counts.
c1286: Thawing at room temperature, in standing water or under warm running water.
c1287: Serving fish raw, marinated or partly cooked without documented parasite destruction.
c1288: Saying an item "contains no" allergen without having checked it in the matrix, or having no allergen guide.
c1289: Handwashing sink used as a utility sink, with no soap, no single-use paper towels or no foot-pedal trash can.
c1290: Cleaning products next to food, or poured into unlabeled bottles.
c1291: Severity categories under the FDA Food Code 2022: Priority = the item directly controls a hazard (temperatures, cooking, handwashing, cross-contamination); Priority foundation = it supports a Priority item (written plans, records, training, equipment); Core = general sanitation and facilities. UK: the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme goes from 0 (urgent improvement necessary) to 5 (very good).
c1292: Priority violations that are not corrected, and any imminent health hazard (fire, flood, sewage backup, loss of water or power, suspected outbreak), can lead to suspension of the permit and closure of the establishment (Food Code §8-404.11). Your local or state health department sets the penalties.
c1293: This guide is a readiness self-check, not an official finding: the category of a violation is always decided by the health department (UK: the local authority), weighing the risk, intent and repeat violations.
c1294: Choose "✓ Compliant", "⚠ Needs work" or "✗ Not compliant". The summary matches the exact text, so anything typed by hand is not counted.
c1302: This is the monitoring log for the CCP of cooking and reheating prepared food. The hazard analysis (template 12 (HACCP Plan Template: Hazard Analysis & CCPs)) points here: without this sheet, the most important CCP in the kitchen had nowhere to be documented.
c1304: ▸ One line per dish cooked or reheated. You do not need to measure every portion: measure the piece or the pan.
c1305: ▸ Measure at the GEOMETRIC CENTER (the thickest part) of the item, with a clean, sanitized probe, and wait for the reading to settle.
c1306: ▸ Record which probe you used. Its monthly check goes in template 19 (Thermometer Calibration Log).
c1307: ▸ The "Status" column calculates itself: OK in green when the center reaches the limit printed in the process name (165, 155, 145 or 135 °F), REPEAT in red below it. For reheating it also checks the time: more than 120 minutes to reach 165 °F is REPEAT even if it gets there.
c1308: ▸ Cooking: reach the limit of the process in the CENTER of the product. 165 °F for poultry and stuffed foods, 155 °F for ground meat and eggs held hot, 145 °F for steaks, fish and eggs cooked to order, 135 °F for vegetables for hot holding (Food Code §3-401.11, §3-401.13).
c1309: ▸ Reheating: 165 °F in the center AND reached within 2 hours (§3-403.11). It is the critical limit that your hazard analysis (template 12 (HACCP Plan Template: Hazard Analysis & CCPs)) declares for this CCP.
c1310: ▸ Why one limit for each food: the Food Code sets a different minimum cooking temperature for each type of food, and 165 °F for reheating. The drop-down shows the limit in the name of each process, so every dish is checked against its own figure. If your own HACCP plan sets a stricter limit, follow your plan. UK: follow the limits in your HACCP plan (Safer Food Better Business).
c1311: ▸ Fish that will be eaten raw, marinated or lightly cured is not cooked, it is frozen. That control goes in template 18 (Parasite Destruction Log (Fish Served Raw)).
c1312: ▸ Frequency: every dish cooked or reheated that your hazard analysis marks as a CCP. The sheet has 40 rows.
c1327: Criterion of the sheet: reach the limit shown in the process name in the CENTER of the item. If it says REPEAT, reheat it until it gets there and record the action; an item is never served while its verdict is red.
c1328: For reheating the verdict ALSO looks at time: if it takes more than 120 minutes to reach 165 °F, it says REPEAT even if it gets there. The product has spent too long in the danger zone.
c1329: The FDA Food Code sets minimum internal cooking temperatures by type of food (§3-401.11, §3-401.13) and 165 °F within 2 hours for reheating (§3-403.11). This kit applies those limits, which are also the critical limits in the hazard analysis (template 12 (HACCP Plan Template: Hazard Analysis & CCPs)). UK: use the limits of your own HACCP plan.

c1433: The whole kit decides with temperatures, and every temperature comes from a thermometer. If the thermometer is off, the temperature, cooking, cooling and parasite destruction logs prove the opposite of what happened. c1434: ▸ One line per thermometer or probe and per check. Number your equipment and always use the same number in the other logs.
c1435: ▸ Enter the ELEVATION of your kitchen in feet in the green cell of the header (B3) before anything else. It only affects the boiling-point method, but without it a perfect probe can come out FAIL: in Denver, at 5,280 ft, water boils at about 202 °F.
c1436: ▸ Pick the method from the drop-down. The "Reference" fills itself: 32 °F with an ice bath and 212 minus elevation / 550 with boiling water.
c1437: ▸ Enter the reading of the device. The "Deviation" and the "Status" calculate themselves: PASS in green up to ±2 °F, FAIL in red above that.
c1438: The two methods, step by step
c1439: ▸ Ice point: fill a glass with crushed ice, add cold water just to cover it, stir, wait two minutes and measure in the center without touching the glass. It must read 32 °F ±2.
c1440: ▸ Boiling point: water at a rolling boil, measure in the center. It must read the "Reference" the sheet calculates ±2 °F, which is 212 °F at sea level and about 202 °F at 5,280 ft. If you are not sure of your elevation, use the ice point.
c1441: What to do with a FAIL
c1442: ▸ Recalibrate the device if it has an adjustment, or take it out of use and replace it.
c1443: ▸ Review the records taken with that device since its last good check: they may be wrong and you have to assess whether they affected any product (template 11 (Corrective Action Log)).
c1444: ▸ Recommended frequency: monthly for each thermometer and probe, and always after a knock or a drop. The sheet has 40 rows: a year for three or four devices.
c1445: Year: _______________    One monthly check for each thermometer and probe in the establishment. Tolerance: ±2 °F.

c1460: Ice-point method: fill a glass with crushed ice and add a little cold water to cover it; stir, wait two minutes and measure in the center without touching the bottom or the sides. The reference is 32 °F.
c1461: Boiling-point method: water at a rolling boil. The reference is NOT always 212 °F: water boils about 1 °F lower for every 550 ft of elevation. Enter the elevation of your kitchen in the green cell above (B3) and the "Reference" column corrects itself: in Denver (5,280 ft) it becomes about 202 °F. If you do not know it, use the ice point, which does not depend on elevation.

c1528: What differs from what is usually done
c1529: When you suspect that a food is harmful, the first move is not to call 911: it is to pull the product and notify your local or state health department right away, and to follow the recall notices from the FDA and USDA. The health department coordinates the response with the state and federal agencies. Call 911 only if someone has symptoms; Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222. UK: tell your local authority and the FSA right away; NHS 111 for health advice and 999 in an emergency.
c1531: ▸ You receive a recall notice from your supplier, the FDA, the USDA or the health department.
c1532: ▸ You find a spoiled or unsafe product that has already been used or served.
c1533: ▸ A customer reports feeling ill in a way that may be linked to something you served.
c1534: ▸ The cold chain breaks on a lot that has already been distributed or served.
c1536: ▸ Template 06 (Food Traceability Log (Lots In & Out)): to find out where the lot came from and which dishes and services it went to.
c1537: ▸ Template 11 (Corrective Action Log): that is where the incident and the fate of the noncompliant product are documented.
c1538: FOOD RECALL & FOODBORNE ILLNESS RESPONSE PLAN
c1539: Follow these steps IN ORDER. Do not improvise. Hang this poster in a visible spot in the kitchen.
c1541: Identify the affected product: name, lot no., supplier and date received.
c1542: Check template 06 (Food Traceability Log (Lots In & Out)) (lots in and out).
c1544: Pull the product from the food chain IMMEDIATELY. Do not serve it, do not cook it, do not put it back in general storage.
c1545: Tag it "DO NOT USE - ALERT" and set it apart in an isolated, labeled area.
c1547: Notify your local or state health department and the supplier right away. If a food you have served may be unsafe, the health department coordinates the response and you follow the recall notices from the FDA and USDA. UK: tell your local authority and the FSA right away.
c1548: Call 911 ONLY if someone has symptoms: it is a medical emergency, not the channel for reporting a recall. Also tell the quality manager or the general manager. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222.
c1550: Record which product it is, how much is left in stock, how much has been served and to whom.
c1551: Complete the corrective action log (template 11 (Corrective Action Log)) with the incident number.
c1553: If the product was served to the public, inform the affected customers you can identify and follow the instructions of the health department.
c1554: Coordinate with the supplier to pull and return the product.
c1556: Check that no affected product remains anywhere on the premises.
c1557: Check coolers, freezers, storeroom, dining room, mise en place and work in progress.
c1559: Document the whole process: dates, times, actions, people involved and outcome.
c1560: File it with the corrective action log (template 11 (Corrective Action Log)) and review whether any procedure has to change so it does not happen again.
c1562: Local or state health department (UK: your local authority and the FSA)

c1571: Basis: FSMA 204 (traceability records to the FDA within 24 hours for foods on the Food Traceability List, required from July 20, 2028), shellstock tags kept 90 days (§3-203.12) and the recall notices of the FDA and USDA. UK: if you suspect that a food you have placed on the market may be unsafe, withdraw it and tell your local authority and the FSA right away. 911 (UK: 999) is for medical emergencies and does not replace that notification.
c1572: Print this poster on US Letter paper (or enlarge it to 11 x 17 in from the print dialog of your printer) and hang it in a visible spot in the kitchen. All staff must know it.
